18.0.0.en: 1 The word of the LORD came unto me again, saying, 2 "What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge? 3 As I live, saith the Lord GOD, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel. 4 Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die. 5 But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right, 6 And hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, neither hath defiled his neighbour's wife, neither hath come near to a menstruous woman, 7 And hath not oppressed any, but hath restored to the debtor his pledge, hath spoiled none by violence, hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment; 8 He that hath not given forth upon usury, neither hath taken any increase, that hath withdrawn his hand from iniquity, hath executed true judgment between man and man, 9 Hath walked in my statutes, and hath kept my judgments, to deal truly; he is just, he shall surely live, saith the Lord GOD.

18.1.0.en: In this chapter the Lord dealt with the proverb that was common among the Jewish people: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" [2]. They felt that the divine wrath that came upon them was only the fruit of the evil of their fathers, who had brought idol worship into the divine sanctuaries. But the Lord wanted to affirm that He will not recompense a man for the sins of his parents, and that the discipline He permits is because of what people do in their own time.

18.1.1.en: We dealt with this subject earlier, in the commentary on the Book of Exodus, where the Lord says, "For I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me" (Ex 20:5). We saw that God does not mean by this that He makes one generation bear the sins of the former generations; rather, in His love He is longsuffering toward one generation and a second, that perhaps they may repent. If they do not repent, He makes the third generation, and the fourth as well, bear the discipline, because they did not repent through their fathers, since He calls them "them that hate me." But if they repent through their fathers, they are not counted as sons of the wicked; rather God Himself becomes their Father, and they enjoy His grace.

18.1.2.en: * The soul that does not dwell in God is the source of its own evils, so it sins, and the soul that sins is the one that dies.

18.2.0.en: St. Ambrose: There is no partiality with God; the soul of the father is as the soul of the son, or as He says: "Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die" [4]... Here we ask:

18.2.1.en: First: Does a man inherit nothing of the weaknesses of his father?

18.3.s.en: First: Does a man inherit nothing of the weaknesses of his father?

18.3.0.en: The Holy Bible does not ignore the effect of parents on a person's life. A person who is born in a holy home and brought up between godly parents finds a possibility that helps the growth of his spiritual life and the setting out of his soul to live with God. On the contrary, if he has a wicked father and a wicked mother, then even if they do not encourage their son to sin and evil, at the very least they stand as a stumbling block before his spiritual growth. Nevertheless, many children loved evil in spite of the godliness of their parents, such as the two sons of Eli the priest, and there are also children who loved righteousness in spite of the evil of their fathers. The environment in which a person lives may be good or evil, but it does not compel him to goodness or evil. Indeed, a man himself may begin his life with evil and then return and complete his way with God, and he may begin in the Spirit and then fall back into evil and live in sin. For this reason this chapter has presented to us four examples: one who was wicked though his father was righteous, one who was righteous though his father was wicked, and one who was righteous and then turned aside, or the opposite. This happened in the kings of Judah. Hezekiah the good king was a consecrated servant, who "did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done" (2 Chr 29:2); he opened his reign by repairing and cleansing the Temple, removed the high places and cast out the images... But his father Ahaz had his heart attached to the love of idols from the beginning of his reign, made his son pass through the fire and sacrificed on the high places (2 Kgs 16:3-4); indeed he shut up the doors of the porch of the Temple, put out the lamps, and burned no incense nor offered burnt offerings to the living God (2 Chr 29:7). As for Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, he led his people astray from the truth, and made them sacrifice to all the host of heaven, and they did worse than the nations whom the LORD had destroyed before the children of Israel (2 Kgs 21:2-9), although in the last of his days he amended much of what he had corrupted (2 Chr 33:1-20).

18.4.0.en: St. Jerome distinguishes between the saying of the Psalmist: "What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death?" (Ps 89:48), and what is said by Ezekiel the prophet: "The soul that sinneth, it shall die" [4], saying: [There is a difference between seeing death and tasting it, for he who sees, sees indeed but does not taste it, while he who tastes it of necessity sees it]. By this he means that all mankind sees death, the death of the body, but he whose soul is sanctified in the Lord sees the death of his body yet does not taste death, since he bears the power of Christ's resurrection working in him.

18.4.1.en: * As there is a death of the body, there is a death of the soul... The death of the soul is in any case not like the death of the body; it is utterly dreadful. The death of the body is the separation of the soul from the body, the one from the other, so that man is released from pending cares and toils, and the other (the soul) is transferred to a clear dwelling. Then, when the body is dissolved and decomposes, it is gathered together again in incorruption and receives its soul back again. This is the death of the body, but the death of the soul is fearful and terrifying. In it, when dissolution takes place, the soul does not come to an end as the body does, but is joined to the body again and is not annihilated; it is cast with it into the fire that is not quenched.

18.4.2.en: St. John Chrysostom: * This death (of the soul) has as its opponent and enemy Him who said: "I am the life" (Jn 14:6).

18.4.3.en: Origen: * According to the Holy Scriptures we learn that there are three kinds of death:

18.4.4.en: A death when we die to sin and live to God. Blessed is this death by which we flee from sin and are consecrated to God, for it separates us from what is mortal and sanctifies us to Him who is immortal.

18.4.5.en: The other death is the departure from this life, as the father Abraham and the father David died and were buried with their fathers, when the soul is freed from the bonds of the body.

18.4.6.en: The third death is that of which it was said, "Let the dead bury their dead" (Mt 8:22). By this death not only the body dies but the soul also, for "the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ezek 18:4); it dies to the Lord, not through the weakness of nature but through the weakness of committing transgression. This death is not a leaving of this life but a falling into error.

18.4.7.en: Therefore spiritual death is one thing, natural death another, and the third is death as punishment.

18.4.8.en: St. Ambrose: St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the words found in this chapter [4-9] "contain a description of the conduct of Christians, in which God nobly urges us to the blessed life, which is the reward of a life of goodness, eternal life." This description includes the positive and negative aspects in the life of the believer:

18.5.0.en: A. It befits the Christian to walk in righteousness, to do that which is lawful and right [5], not to eat upon the mountains that were defiled by the sacrifices of the idolaters, nor to lift up his eyes to their idols. Thus he is sanctified entirely: he is sanctified in his heart by righteousness, truth and justice, and sanctified in his eating by refraining from taking part in pagan feasts, and sanctified even in the glances of his eyes, so that he does not lift up his eyes to their idols. He is sanctified by the positive work, which is doing righteousness and loving truth and justice, and negatively by refraining from everything that is evil...

18.5.1.en: B. The Christian does not defile his neighbour's wife, nor does he come near his own wife when she is menstruous; he loves holiness in his inner life and in his body as in others; he does not covet his brother's wife...

18.6.0.en: C. He does not practice injustice against anyone, not only by giving others their lawful rights, but he gives the poor man his right in sharing his needs, and gives the naked man his right in sharing his clothes with him, and offers the needy debtor the right of love and mercy, so that he demands no usury from him, and he offers others the right of supporting the wronged against the wrongdoer, so that he does not stand by passively but "hath executed true judgment between man and man" [8].

18.7.0.en: D. The secret of his righteous life is his entering into the divine commandment, as the Lord says: "Hath walked in my statutes, and hath kept my judgments, to deal truly; he is just" [9].

18.8.s.en: 2. A wicked son of a righteous father:

18.8.0.en: 10 "If he beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, and that doeth the like to any one of these things, 11 And that doeth not any of those duties, but even hath eaten upon the mountains, and defiled his neighbour's wife, 12 Hath oppressed the poor and needy, hath spoiled by violence, hath not restored the pledge, and hath lifted up his eyes to the idols, hath committed abomination, 13 Hath given forth upon usury, and hath taken increase: shall he then live? he shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him.

18.9.0.en: The first example the Lord gave concerning personal responsibility is the wicked son of the righteous father. He "shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him" [13]. His father's righteousness does not rescue him from the fruit of his abominations, but he shall surely die.

18.9.1.en: St. Jerome wrote to the deacon Sabinianus, urging him to repent, as follows: [Perhaps you are deluded in yourself that the bishop who ordained you is a holy man, and you think that his merits atone for your transgressions. I have already told you that the father is not punished for his son, nor the son for his father. The soul that sinneth, it shall die].

18.10.s.en: 3. A righteous son of a wicked father:

18.10.0.en: 14 "Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like, 15 That hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, hath not defiled his neighbour's wife, 16 Neither hath oppressed any, hath not withholden the pledge, neither hath spoiled by violence, but hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment, 17 That hath taken off his hand from the poor, that hath not received usury nor increase, hath executed my judgments, hath walked in my statutes; he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live. 18 As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, spoiled his brother by violence, and did that which is not good among his people, lo, even he shall die in his iniquity. 19 Yet say ye, Why? doth not the son bear the iniquity of the father? When the son hath done that which is lawful and right, and hath kept all my statutes, and hath done them, he shall surely live. 20 The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

18.10.1.en: The people in the days of King Zedekiah thought that they were more righteous than the people in the days of King Manasseh, so they felt that they were bearing the iniquity of their fathers. But the Lord affirms here: "If he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like... he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live. As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, spoiled his brother by violence, and did that which is not good among his people, lo, even he shall die in his iniquity" [14-19].

18.10.2.en: When a man commits iniquity he loses his life, as St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [Sin is nothing but estrangement from God, who alone is the true life].

18.10.3.en: But perhaps some will ask: How does the righteous son not bear the iniquity of his father when it has been said: "Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered with the LORD; and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out" (Ps 109:14)?

18.10.4.en: St. Augustine answers: [Is it to be understood that even the iniquity of his fathers comes upon a man? Those who are converted in Christ do not have the iniquity of their fathers come upon them, since they are no longer sons of the wicked, because they did not imitate their conduct. Therefore it is added to the words: "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children... of them that hate me" (Ex 20:5), that is, those who hate me as their fathers hated me].

18.11.s.en: 4. A man's turning from his evil:

18.11.0.en: 21 "But if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. 22 All his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him: in his righteousness that he hath done he shall live. 23 Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live? 24 But when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and doeth according to all the abominations that the wicked man doeth, shall he live? All his righteousness that he hath done shall not be mentioned: in his trespass that he hath trespassed, and in his sin that he hath sinned, in them shall he die. 25 Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal? 26 When a righteous man turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and dieth in them; for his iniquity that he hath done shall he die. 27 Again, when the wicked man turneth away from his wickedness that he hath committed, and doeth that which is lawful and right, he shall save his soul alive. 28 Because he considereth, and turneth away from all his transgressions that he hath committed, he shall surely live, he shall not die. 29 Yet saith the house of Israel, The way of the Lord is not equal. O house of Israel, are not my ways equal? are not your ways unequal? 30 Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, saith the Lord GOD. Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin. 31 Cast away from you all your transgressions, whereby ye have transgressed; and make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel? 32 For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye.

18.11.1.en: We have said that the Lord wanted by His speech here to move His people toward repentance, that they should not be troubled because of the sins of their fathers, and also that they should not be troubled by their own previous or present personal sins if they offer true repentance, for He says: "If the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die" [21]. Some consider this statement the center of the whole book, the most precious statement found in it; it is a powerful call to repentance! "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" [23]. He opens the door of hope wide, so that not one soul may perish in a spirit of deadly despair.

18.11.2.en: The Fathers of the Church found in this chapter a fertile field into which every fallen, despairing person may enter to eat of the fruit of repentance and be filled with hope, while it also gives clear warnings to the souls that stand, lest by their negligence they lose all their past labor. The following are some comments of the Fathers:

18.11.3.en: * By encouragement He lightens the weight of sins and lessens the passions, inspiring hope of salvation.

18.11.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria: * For those who are in danger of despair He provided the refuge of forgiveness, and for those who are in danger of (presumptuous) hope, who delay by putting off, He made the day of death uncertain.

18.11.5.en: St. Augustine: * If they hear this voice and believe it, they will be healed of despair and rise from the bottomless pit of depths into which they have fallen.

18.11.6.en: St. Augustine: * We do not despair of any man as long as God's longsuffering leads the wicked to repentance, so we do not drive him out of this life.

18.11.7.en: St. Augustine: * Do not despair of salvation. Remember what is written in the Holy Scripture, that he who falls arises and he who strays returns (Jer 8:4), and the wounded is healed, and he who fell prey to the beasts escapes, and he who confesses his sins is not despised... It is a time for endurance and longsuffering, a time for healing and correction. Have you stumbled? Arise! Have you sinned? Cease from sin!

18.11.8.en: St. Augustine: * Repentance is a "life" better than death...

18.11.9.en: Hasten to it, O sinner, and embrace it as a drowning man embraces some planks, so that it may snatch you from drowning amid the waves of sins and carry you to the divine harbor, full of tenderness.

18.11.10.en: Tertullian: * Since what the Lord says is true, when I repent He forgets all my past sins and all my iniquities; why do you frighten me?

18.11.11.en: God promises me forgiveness; would you cast me into despair?

18.12.0.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles: At the very time when He opens the doors of hope with all power before sinners that they may repent, He warns those who stand lest they fall, saying: "But when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and doeth according to all the abominations that the wicked man doeth, shall he live? All his righteousness that he hath done shall not be mentioned: in his trespass that he hath trespassed, and in his sin that he hath sinned, in them shall he die" [24]. And as St. Anba Anthony says: [Let us persevere in our training every day, knowing that if we neglect it for one single day the Lord will not forgive us for the sake of the past, but will bring His wrath upon our negligence... for Judas ruined his past striving because of one night].

18.12.1.en: And St. Basil the Great says: [When a change occurs, the labor of the righteous becomes vain, just as the sinner is not blamed, by the first turning away from what is good to what is worse, and the second inclining from what is evil to what is better].

18.12.2.en: But is not this statement harsh and severe? St. John Chrysostom answers: [Even in this matter God showed the greatness of the tenderness of His love, presenting to us these terrifying things in order to raise us up and awaken in us a desire for the Kingdom]. And St. Clement of Alexandria says: [The punishments of God are for salvation, and discipline leads us to repentance, for God longs for repentance more than for the death of the sinner].

18.13.0.en: "For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye" [32].

18.13.1.en: God speaks these words to you if you are wretched: "For I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked."

18.13.2.en: Even if you want your own death, I do not want it.

18.13.3.en: You did not create yourself, but by despair you perish.

18.13.4.en: In any case, God created you when you did not exist; afterward He sought you when you went astray, and found you through the blood of His Son and saved you.

18.13.5.en: He Himself calls you: Return from the abyss of despair. Come, for I do not desire the death of the sinner but that he return and live...

18.13.6.en: Do not lose confidence through despair about your sins, and at the same time do not trust in length of life. Therefore repent... Why do you not repent today?

18.13.7.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles: Origen sees in this divine speech concerning the possibility of sinners' returning to God and the warning of those who stand against falling, a confirmation of the error of those who say that there are different natures created thus, showing that the sinner can become good and the opposite.

18.13.8.en: You did not create me to die!

18.13.9.en: * You created me to live in the world as a king, in my royal palace!

18.13.10.en: You did not create me to die, but to live by You and with You!

18.13.11.en: * You are wonderful, O Lord, in Your love for me, for even if I seek death, You desire my life!

18.13.12.en: I do not know what is for my edification and my glory!

18.13.13.en: But You know all that is for my life, O my Creator!

18.13.14.en: * You do not will my death but my life; You do not hold me accountable for the errors of my fathers, nor wound my feelings for sins I have left behind. You are wonderful in Your care for me!

18.13.15.en: * You are the Savior of souls from corruption; You alone are able to renew my nature, O my Savior!
